reference.source: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
clinicalPearls: An anomalous eye movement in which the non-fixating or occluded eye drifts slowly upward, and often extorts, then returns downward when fixation is resumed; because it violates Hering's law it is not a true hypertropia
Strongly associated with early-onset (infantile) esotropia and frequently accompanied by latent nystagmus, inferior oblique overaction and an abnormal head posture

It is typically bilateral though often asymmetric: either eye elevates under cover, unlike a genuine unilateral hypertropia where covering either eye gives reciprocal movements consistent with Hering's law
The hallmark on cover testing is that the covered eye elevates and, on uncovering, re-fixates and moves down without any corresponding downward movement of the fellow eye
It frequently has no fixed measurement, being variable and dissociated, and may be brought out by fatigue or dissociation, with a Bielschowsky darkening phenomenon sometimes demonstrable

It is usually asymptomatic and well controlled, so treatment (superior rectus recession or inferior oblique anterior transposition) is reserved for manifest, cosmetically or functionally significant deviations

Distinguishing it from inferior oblique overaction is important: DVD elevates regardless of horizontal gaze and without a true contralateral hypotropia, whereas inferior oblique overaction elevates in adduction and obeys Hering's law
It commonly coexists with other features of the infantile strabismus complex, so latent nystagmus and horizontal motility anomalies should be sought
reference.pathophysiology: Dissociated vertical deviation is an innervational anomaly that usually arises in the context of disrupted binocular development from early-onset strabismus. The upward drift of the covered or non-fixating eye does not obey Hering's law of equal innervation, indicating that it is not a simple vertical muscle imbalance but a dissociated, supranuclear innervational phenomenon. It has been linked to primitive dorsal light and righting reflexes and to the abnormal binocular development seen with infantile esotropia and latent nystagmus. The magnitude of the deviation is modulated by the degree of dissociation between the two eyes, for example under occlusion or with reduced visual input to one eye.
additionalDifferentials: Inferior oblique overaction (key distinction, as it obeys Hering's law)
True hypertropia from a vertical muscle palsy
Superior oblique palsy with a compensatory head tilt
Other causes of vertical strabismus and incomitance
Craniofacial or orbital causes of a vertical deviation
additionalInvestigations: Alternate cover testing, observing the covered eye elevate and the uncovered eye re-fixate downward
Assessment in all positions of gaze to separate DVD from inferior oblique overaction
Documentation of any associated latent nystagmus and abnormal head posture
Attempted prism measurement, recognising the inherent variability, and testing under different fixation conditions
Assessment of the associated horizontal deviation, usually an infantile esotropia
Fundus torsion assessment and full orthoptic evaluation
redFlags: An acquired vertical deviation with neurological symptoms, prompting reconsideration of a paretic or central cause
A constant large manifest deviation causing symptoms or poor cosmesis
Diplopia, which is unusual in DVD and warrants reassessment
reference.prognosis: DVD is usually benign and often subclinical, controlled by the child without symptoms; when manifest and significant, surgery reduces the deviation although it may not abolish it and can recur or require further procedures. It does not itself threaten vision beyond the amblyopia associated with the underlying infantile strabismus.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing DVD as a simple hypertropia and planning inappropriate surgery
Confusing DVD with inferior oblique overaction by not testing adherence to Hering's law
Expecting a fixed, reproducible measurement when the deviation is inherently variable
Overlooking the associated latent nystagmus and infantile esotropia
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
von Noorden's Binocular Vision and Ocular Motility
management: Observe the many latent, well-controlled, asymptomatic cases without intervention
Treat associated amblyopia and correct refractive error to optimise fixation
Reserve surgery for manifest, cosmetically or functionally significant deviation, using superior rectus recession or inferior oblique anterior transposition
Address coexisting infantile esotropia and inferior oblique overaction at the same surgical setting
Manage associated latent nystagmus and abnormal head posture
Maintain orthoptic follow-up, recognising the inherent variability and the potential for recurrence or need for further surgery
